The University undertakes no responsibility with respect to such Inventions; however, the Inventor may assign the Inventors interest in the Invention to the University, subject to the Universitys acceptance of such assignment.
In the event of an accepted assignment, the invention will be managed as a University-sponsored Invention under this Policy.
It is the responsibility of the Inventor to demonstrate to the University Intellectual Property Committee that University facilities were not involved in any Inventor-retained invention.

The University will not construe the payment of salary, nor the provision of office or library facilities as constituting use of University facilities; however, any assistance that is more than incidental assistance provided by one or more faculty, staff, or students to an Inventor specifically pertaining to the Invention will constitute use of University Facilities.

University Personnel engaged in consulting or business activities must ensure that their agreements with other parties do not conflict with this or any other University Policy or with the Universitys commitments to external Sponsors.
University Personnel must make clear to those with whom they make such agreements their obligations to the University and should apprise other parties of the terms of this Policy.
The Universitys rights and the employees obligations under this Policy will in no way be abrogated or limited by the terms of such third party agreements.

Status Active PolicyStatID 11345907 Last 12/13/2022 Owner Michael Lewis, Approved Ph.D. Next Review 12/12/2025 Document Provost Area Applicability Saint Louis University Campus Wide Intellectual Property Ownership Policy Policy Owner: Provost/Michael Lewis, Ph.D. Responsible University Official: Provost/Michael Lewis, Ph.D. Policy Contact: Provost/Michael Lewis, Ph.D. 1.0 Reason for Policy This policy governs the ownership of Intellectual Property created at Saint Louis University.
The purpose of this policy is to define the respective ownership rights of the University and its personnel, relative to Intellectual Property resulting from University activities.
2.0 Policy Statement For purposes of this Policy, Intellectual Property is divided into two categories: Technical Works and Creative Works.

Technical Works are patented or unpatented inventions, devices, machines, processes, methods, compositions, research materials, computer software, collections/repositories, industrial designs, databases, technical drawings, biogenic materials, novel chemical matter, lab notebooks and other research data, or human tissues or other samples.
Intellectual Property rights in Technical Works are generally protected through Patents.
Creators of Technical Works are referred to as Inventors for purposes of this Policy.

Creative Works are Intellectual Property not covered in Technical Works that are of an artistic, scholarly, instructional, assessment, or entertainment nature, such as creative productions, musical scores, books, poems, films, video and audio recordings, and instructional materials, such as textbooks and multimedia programs, and names, designs and logos that represent a particular product or service.
Intellectual Property rights in Creative Works are generally protected through Copyright and Trademark.
Creators of Creative Works are referred to as Authors for purposes of this Policy.

The University owns all rights, title, and interest in and to Technical Works and Creative Works that are Works-for-hire as defined in this policy to include those Works that are created as an assigned University duty, created with the intent to be used by multiple University personnel, or for which the University has entered into a written agreement with the Inventor/Author for ownership to vest with the University; arise out of research sponsored by an external entity, such as a federal agency, foundation, or company, and will transfer such ownership in accordance with any sponsor requirements; or arise out of significant use of funds or facilities administered by the University.

As a condition of employment or other involvement in University activities, University Personnel agree to abide by this policy and hereby assign and agree to assign to the University all of their rights, title and interest in and to any and all Technical Works and Creative Works described above.
The University has sole control over the transfer of any rights or ownership of University-owned Technical Works and Creative Works.
University Personnel, other than the Provost or a designee, have no authority to transfer any right, title or interest in University-owned Technical Works and Creative Works to a third party.

The University does not claim ownership of the following Intellectual Property: Copyright in student theses or dissertations; Technical Works and Creative Works that are produced as a normal outcome of scholarly work, in any format, including professional papers published in scholarly journals, monographs of an academic nature, textbooks, artistic creations or performances, course materials, curricula and syllabi, with the exception of Works-for-hire; Technical Works and Creative Works developed on the personal, unpaid time of University Personnel and without use of University facilities; Technical Works and Creative Works developed by students to earn credit in University courses or otherwise satisfy university degree requirements, except in cases where any research giving rise to such Works is sponsored by an external entity or is undertaken by the student in their role as a graduate assistant or paid employee of the University; Technical Works and Creative Works arising out of use of the University facilities that have been rented or leased by an outside entity to which the University has relinquished any rights in such Works by written agreement.

The Inventor/Author of a non-University-owned Technical Work or Creative Work that falls under a category in Section E above may request from the University written confirmation that the University does not claim ownership of such Work.

The request shall be made in writing and directed to the Provost and must include a description of the Technical Work or Creative Work and facts supporting the Inventor/Author's assertion of non-University ownership.

The Provost will consult with the Office of the General Counsel and communicate to the Author/Inventor whether the University claims ownership of the Technical Work or Creative Work as described in the Inventor/Author's written request.

The Inventor(s)/Author(s) may not make use of University resources or use the name or logos of the University, other than factual statements regarding their student or employee status, in exploiting any non-University-owned Work.
The Provost may waive the University's interests in a Technical Work or Creative Work.
Typically, this decision will be reached because the Provost or a designee believes that future investment of University resources is not justified by a cost/benefit analysis.
The Provost or a designee shall communicate in writing to the Inventor/Author the University's decision to waive title to the Work.
At that time, the Inventor/Author may elect to seek title to the Work, which would culminate in a Return of IP Agreement between the Inventor/Author and the University.

Terms for a Return of IP Agreement will be negotiated by the Provost or a designee and the Inventor/Author, retaining, on behalf of the University, rights to use the Work in connection with research and teaching.

For purposes of this policy, significant use of University resources in the production of a Technical or Creative Work includes, but is not limited to, the following: Use of university facilities such as laboratories, studios, equipment, production facilities, or specialized computing resources in excess of what is routinely made available to University faculty, staff or students; University funding in support of the Work's creation; Direct assignment or commission from the University to undertake a creative project or research project as a part of the Inventor/Author's regular appointment; More than minimal use of funding from gifts to the University to support creation of the Works involved; Production of the Work under specific terms of a sponsored research grant or contract; Use of specifically designated University funds or extensive use of the services of a support unit financed by the University for production of a Work.

2.0 Policy Statement University Personnel are required to provide notification of each University-owned Technical Work and all Commercializable Creative Works to the University office designated by the VPR through a disclosure process as prescribed by this policy.
The Office of the Vice President for Research (OVPR) shall have the responsibility for the protection of all University-owned Technical Works and Commercializable Creative Works.

All Inventor(s)/Author(s) shall provide to the OVPR such additional information or materials as it may request in support of securing Intellectual Property protection, including the registration of copyrights and the filing and prosecution of patent applications.

In accordance with the University's IP Ownership Policy, at any time after disclosure of a Technical Work or Commercializable Creative Work, the Provost may waive the University's interests in a Technical Work or Creative Work.

The Vice President for Research (VPR) is the Provost's designee for communications to Inventors/Authors regarding the University's decision to waive title to a Technical Work or Commercializable Creative Work.

At that time, the Inventor/Author may elect to seek title to the Technical Work or Commercializable Creative Work, which would culminate in a Return of IP Agreement between the Inventor/Author and the University.

Terms for a Return of IP Agreement will be negotiated by the VPR (or an appropriate designee) and the Inventor/Author, retaining, on behalf of the University, rights to use the Invention in connection with research and teaching.
The OVPR is the designee of the Provost given sole responsibility for the Commercialization or other transfer of all University-owned Technical Works and Commercializable Creative Works.
It is anticipated that the Inventor(s)/Author(s) of such Works will be an active participant in the Commercialization process and shall be kept informed by OVPR of its Commercialization efforts.

Such efforts will generally include researching the commercial market for the Technical or Creative Work, entering into discussions with potential licensees, negotiating appropriate Licenses or other agreements, monitoring progress of licensees, and distributing Commercialization Income pursuant to this policy.
The OVPR will comply with any and all contractual obligations regarding the transfer of Intellectual Property included in any research funding agreement.
The transfer of University-owned Technical and Creative Works by the OVPR may also take the form of a sale, gift or donation, or placing such Work into the public domain.
The OVPR is the designee of the Provost given sole responsibility for the management of all transfers of Research Materials, whether incoming or outgoing, between the University and outside parties.
Transfers to or from non-profit entities are generally made through a Research Materials Transfer Agreement.
Transfers to or from a for-profit entity are generally made through a License.
No transfers of Research Materials shall be made by University Personnel without the written authorization of the VPR (or an appropriate designee).
All revenues derived from the Commercialization of University-owned Technical Works and Creative Works will be received and administered by the OVPR.

Net Commercialization Income means the gross revenues received by the University from the commercialization of University Intellectual Property less any and all expenses related to the Intellectual Property paid by the University including, without limitation, all patent-related costs, legal defense and enforcement action costs, and marketing and licensing costs for said Intellectual Property.

Net Commercialization Income shall be distributed according to the schedule shown below: 40% to the Inventor(s)/Author(s) collectively, 15% to the Inventor/Author's Department(s), 15% to the Inventor/Author's College(s) or Institutional Unit(s), and 30% to the Office of the Vice President for Research.

In the event of two or more Inventors/Authors, all Inventors/Authors will execute a binding agreement promptly after disclosure of a Technical Work or Creative Work that will delineate each Inventor/Author's personal share (percentage) of Commercialization Income.
Inventors/Authors shall have the right to waive their personal share of Commercialization Income to their laboratory or department.
The University assumes no responsibility or liability in disputes among Inventors/Authors concerning the sharing of Commercialization Income.

If Inventors/Authors are from multiple University departments, colleges or units, the applicable share of Commercialization Income will be divided equally between such departments, colleges or Institutional Units, unless an alternative distribution schedule is agreed upon by the heads of the respective departments, colleges and Institutional Units and the VPR.

When Commercialization Income is in the form of equity (stock) interest in a company, the University will, upon occurrence of a liquidation event, distribute cash in accordance with the distribution schedule in Section 10(A)i above.

In some cases, distribution of Commercialization revenue to individual Inventors/Authors will be impractical or inappropriate; for example, where the Work was developed as a departmental project or where the Inventors/Authors are not easily identifiable.
In such situations, subject to the approval of the VPR, the Inventors/Authors share of Commercialization Income shall be distributed to their University department(s).

The right of an Inventor/Author to receive a share of Commercialization Income hereunder shall survive termination of affiliation with the University, and in the event of death of the Inventor/Author shall inure to their estate.
This right may be assigned or bequeathed by the Inventor/Author.
All internal appeals and disputes relating to the Commercialization of University-owned Intellectual Property shall be forwarded in writing to the VPR.
The VPR shall make a final determination concerning an appeal or dispute after receiving written notice of such appeals and/or disputes.
Any disagreement on the part of University Personnel with determinations reached by the VPR shall be submitted in accordance with University grievance policies.

No assignment of rights, transfer of ownership, license, or any other contractual arrangements concerning the Commercialization of University-owned Intellectual Property shall be made without the written authorization of the VPR (or an appropriate designee).

Only the President, Provost, VPR (or an appropriate designee) may commit University funds for the protection of University-owned Intellectual Property in accordance with their respective levels of signature authority.

The aim is to assure that new and useful technologies be made available as products for the public good, and that the Institute and its inventors share in revenues from these products to encourage and support their research and educational efforts.

The Patent Committee consists of the Vice President for Research Services (chair), the Vice President for Finance, one academic dean (chosen on a rotating basis of two-year terms), and two additional members appointed by the President from among the faculty and professional research staff.
The Patent Committee has the responsibility for recommending and approving actions relative to intellectual property rights.

The President and the Vice President for Research Services have recommended, and the Board of Trustees has approved, that the services of the Office of Technology Transfer will be provided to the Institute by Stevens Technologies, Inc. and another affiliated organization, Technology Holdings, LLC.
Stevens Technologies, Inc. is a wholly owned subsidiary of Stevens Institute created to conduct the business of technology transfer for the Institute.

Technology Holdings, LLC provides funding to partially support technology transfer operations and to provide assistance in conceiving, assessing, and obtaining financing for commercial opportunities for the Institute's technologies.

Stevens Technologies, Inc. and Technology Holdings, LLC are organized so that business transactions can be conducted at an "arms length" from Stevens Institute, to mitigate against potential liabilities and to assure compliance with State and Federal tax codes.

The Office of Technology Transfer serves the Stevens community by providing consulting on intellectual property issues, marketing and licensing of intellectual properties, and assistance in commercialization-related initiatives.

This Guide is published to detail Stevens' policies and practices which were instituted to assure that technology transfer and commercialization initiatives are compatible with the educational mission of the Institute.
It also describes the responsibilities of the Patent Committee and the technology transfer services and practices of the Office of Research Services and the Office of Technology Transfer.

Mission for Technology Transfer: To promote the transfer of Stevens technology for society's use and benefit while generating income to support research and education.

TECHNOLOGY AS INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY AND RELATED RIGHTS The term "technology" is broadly defined in this guide to include technical innovations, inventions, and discoveries, as well as writings and other information in various forms, including computer software.

The principal rights governing the ownership and disposition of technology are known as "intellectual property" rights, which are derived primarily from legislation granting patent, copyright, trademark, and integrated circuit mask work protection.
The term "inventor" is generally associated with the person or persons who conceive a patentable technology and whose names are listed on such patents.
The term "author" is generally associated with the person or persons who produce a copyrightable work.
In this Guide, the word inventor will sometimes be used in a generic sense to imply the creator of a technology or writing or other protectable innovation.
This is intended to simplify discussion of certain situations, such as the creation of software, which is both patentable and copyrightable.
In some instances, distribution and commercialization of technology may be accomplished by the transfer or licensing of the intellectual property rights, such as patents and copyrights.

In other instances, distribution and commercialization of technology may be aided by or depend upon access to the physical or tangible embodiment of the technology, as in the case of biological organisms, plant varieties, or computer software.

Therefore, this policy will define not only the ownership and commercialization rights associated with the technology in the form of intellectual property, but will also define policies and procedures which govern use and distribution of the technology in its tangible form.
The following is an overview of intellectual property rights.
The Office of Technology Transfer may be consulted for further information regarding any of these rights.
PATENTS AND PATENT RIGHTS An invention is any possibly patentable device, process, or product.

A patent is a grant issued by the United States Patent and Trademark Office giving an inventor or inventors the right to exclude all others from making, using, or selling the invention within the United States, its territories, and possessions, for a period of 20 years from the effective filing date.
Patents may also be granted in foreign countries; procedures for filing, regulations for patentability, and term of patent grant vary considerably from country to country.
Inventors may assign their ownership rights to others; commonly, employees assign their rights to employers.
To be patentable in most countries, an invention must be new, useful, and non-obvious.
In the United States, a grace period of 12 months from the first public disclosure, use, sale, or offer-to-sell of an invention is allowed for filing a patent application.
In most foreign countries, an invention is unpatentable unless the application is filed before public disclosure (written or oral).

However, if one has filed in the United States prior to disclosure, the applicant has 12 months to file in many foreign countries, with which the United States has treaties, without losing filing rights.

COPYRIGHTS Copyright law provides that a copyright owner has the exclusive right to reproduce the work, prepare derivative works, distribute by sale or otherwise, and display or perform the work publicly.

Under federal copyright law, copyright subsists in "original works of authorship" which have been fixed in any tangible medium of expression from which they can be perceived, reproduced, or otherwise communicated, either directly or with the aid of a machine or device.
For an individual creator, copyright protection of a work extends for the creator's life plus 50 years.
For employers, copyright protection of a work extends for 75 years from the date of publication.

A copyright covers the "artistic expression" in the particular literary work, musical work, computer program, video or motion picture or sound recording, photograph, sculpture, and so forth, in which the "expression" is embodied, illustrated, or explained, but does not protect the "idea."

TRADE AND SERVICE MARKS A trade or service mark is a word, name, symbol, or device (or any combination) adopted by an organization to identify its goods or services and distinguish them from the goods and services of others.
In the United States, trademark ownership is generally acquired through use of a term to identify the origin of goods or services.
Recent legislation, however, enables organizations to file for trademark protection based on intent to use a particular term.
Trade or service mark ownership is not dependent upon federal or state registration, but upon use of the mark.
Registration of trade and service marks may be obtained on both the state and federal levels.
However, to apply for a federal registration of a mark, it must be used in interstate commerce.

MASK WORKS A mask work is defined as a series of related images representing a predetermined, three-dimensional pattern of metallic, insulating, or semiconducting layers of a semiconductor chip product.

Under the Semiconductor Chip 8/7/25, 1:26 PM Wayback Machine Act of 1984, mask work protection extends for 10 years and gives the owner of the qualifying mask work exclusive rights to its exploitation.
Mask works are registered with the United States Copyright Office.
Failure to apply within 2 years of the initial commercial exploitation results in the termination of the exclusive rights.
The term "tangible research property" refers to those research results which are in a tangible form as distinct from intangible (or intellectual) property.

Examples of tangible property include integrated circuit chips, computer software, biological organisms, engineering prototypes, engineering drawings, and other property which can be physically distributed.

Although tangible research property may often have intangible property rights associated with it, such as biological organisms which may be patented or computer software which may be either patented or copyrighted, where appropriate, tangible research property may be distributed without securing intellectual property protection by using some form of contractual agreement, such as formal contract, loan agreement, letter agreement, or user license.
The law of trade secret may be applied to almost any secret which is used in business and gives the owner of the trade secret a competitive edge over others.
It is used to protect valuable proprietary information and is a commonly used form of protection for software.
Unlike copyrights, there is no federal trade secret statute.
Trade secret laws are determined by the individual states but generally adhere to similar principles.
The most important aspect of this type of protection is that of secrecy.
The protection will remain legally valid only as long as a trade secret is maintained.
In order to maintain protection while a trade secret is being used, it is necessary to bind those individuals having access to the secret by a contractual agreement not to disclose it.
Such agreements are called "nondisclosure" or "Confidential Disclosure Agreements."

It is frequently desirable to maintain the secrecy of key components of a technology for which intellectual property protection is being sought, at least until a patent is issued or other rights assurance mechanisms are in place.
It is also frequent that interest in a technology by potential licensees is greatest during this period.
In order for the Institute or an inventor to have substantive discussions with potential licensees, Confidential Disclosure Agreements are executed between Stevens and the potential licensee.
Stevens is the disclosing party in such instances; a standard Stevens Confidential Disclosure Agreement has been designed to meet most contingencies.
OTT will assist with its preparation for each specific application.
During the course of certain sponsored research projects, a third party may find it necessary to disclose confidential material to Stevens researchers.
In these cases, Confidential Disclosure Agreements are executed between Stevens and the third party.
These agreements protect the third party by prohibiting disclosure by Stevens for a period of time, typically three years.
Stevens employees who participate in the associated sponsored research project are legally required to abide by the non-disclosure terms in the executed agreement.
The principal investigator must make colleagues and students aware of this requirement.
Confidential Disclosure Agreements, as with most contracts, are prepared in duplicate.
The originating party sends two copies to the second party for its approval; frequently there is some negotiation as to the details of the language of the agreement.
After approval and agreement, both copies are signed and sent back to the originator.
The originating party signs both and returns one of the signed originals back to the other party.
Thus both have a signed record of the actual agreement.
Confidential disclosure agreements will be negotiated and/or prepared by OTT at the request of either the third party or the principal investigator.
Executed agreements must be signed by the Vice President for Research Services and are kept on file by OTT.
A "license" grants certain rights to intellectual property.

It is generally provided for by a license agreement which is a contract that determines the terms and conditions under which rights are granted to the licensee and specifies any limitations to those rights.
Royalties and fees are normally paid to the owner of the patent or copyright in exchange for the granting of a license.
The license can be exclusive or non-exclusive, depending on whether the licensor retains the right to grant use to additional licensees.
There can be geographic, field-of-use, and other restrictions as well placed on the rights granted.
A "shop right" is usually retained by the licensor as part of each license agreement.

Shop right is defined as a non-exclusive right to make, use, or practice an invention (but not to sell or lease the invention) without payment of royalties to the inventor(s) or their assignees or successors in interest.
License agreements will be prepared and negotiated by OTT, generally in conjunction with the inventor(s) and research laboratories at Stevens.

OTT assists in the commercial development of selected technology by identifying potential markets and negotiating license agreements as described in Section 4.
OTT will also, when appropriate, recommend Stevens' holding equity in a company engaged in the commercialization of one of its technologies.
An overview of the steps that take place during the technology transfer process are given here.
Naturally the beginning is the conception of an invention and the research work that leads up to and confirms the concept.

Once the inventor(s) believes that he or she has invented something, the following occur: A Technology Disclosure is prepared and sent to the Office of Research Services, the disclosure is presented to the Institute Patent Committee which makes a recommendation with regard to the seeking of intellectual property protection, informed by a preliminary evaluation of patentability and/or commercial feasibility made by OTT and the inventor/author, following the approval by the President of the Institute, a patent case is assigned to intellectual property counsel with experience in the base technology of the invention.

If registration of copyright has been recommended by the Patent Committee, the task can normally be handled within OTT, with the assistance of outside counsel if required, the inventor assists patent counsel to prepare, file, and prosecute a patent application, market analysis, commercial potential, and business recommendations are prepared by OTT with the assistance of the inventor, OTT seeks potential licensees or assists in the process of new business formation, Confidential Disclosure Agreements are generally executed with potential licensees; the inventor(s) is closely involved in the disclosure of the invention to them, license management and relationship with licensee is maintained by OTT, OTT provides regular reporting to the President of the Institute, and licenses are managed for Stevens by OTT, including distribution of royalties or other revenues.

Members of the faculty and staff and other employees shall submit a timely written technology disclosure for each invention they have conceived or developed except for inventions resulting from permissible activity carried out without the use of Institute facilities or services.
A Stevens technology disclosure is a written description of the invention.
The disclosure is prepared by the inventor(s) and is based on research records contained in laboratory notebooks.

Notebooks and other records, when properly executed (each page signed/dated by the researcher and also read, understood, and signed/dated by a witness who is not a potential inventor), provide legal verification of invention and inventorship.

The disclosure should be made through a Stevens Technology Disclosure Form which asks questions regarding the nature, utility, novelty, limitations, commercialization, documentation, and any prior forms of disclosure.

The Technology Disclosure Form should also be used for presenting copyrightable materials or mask works.
The completed disclosure is submitted to the Vice President for Research Services.

Once submitted, it will be forwarded by ORS to OTT, which will initiate action to investigate the patenting or other methods of protection and marketing of the technology unless accompanied by a letter requesting other action by Stevens, such as a waiver of Stevens ownership rights in the technology.
The disclosure, along with the results of OTT's initial investigation, are presented to the Patent Committee, normally within 60 days.
This presentation is usually made by the inventor(s) and OTT.

Sponsored programs: The terms of sponsored research and other agreements normally create obligations with respect to the reporting of inventions, technical data, and copyrightable works such as software.
In particular, inventions, copyrightable materials, and mask works developed under sponsored research should be promptly reported by submitting a Technology Disclosure Form.

In order to discharge Stevens' obligations to research sponsors regarding intellectual property rights, including the government, OTT will coordinate with the Office of Sponsored Projects (OSP) in making appropriate notifications regarding the disclosure, as specified in the research agreement or contract which is maintained by OSP.

If the research which spawned the invention was supported by the US Government, it is important that the funding agency be notified of the disclosure (Form: OMB No. 0704-0297) and of the Institute's intent to file for patent protection.
This notification preserves the rights of the Institute and of the inventor(s), subject only to a limitation that the government has a right to use the technology for its purposes.
OTT or OSP can assist with reporting the invention to the government.
All technical reports to the sponsoring agency that contain descriptions of the technology to be protected should be marked "Confidential."
A copy of all reports and publications which relate to or which contain information about a disclosed technology must be submitted to ORS.
OTT may be consulted as to the discretion of publications and/or the proper treatment of disclosed material in reports.

Other programs: Inventions or technology developed under Stevens-administered programs, either as work-for-hire or with significant use of Stevens funds or facilities, should also be submitted using a Technology Disclosure Form.
Independently-owned technology need not be disclosed to Stevens unless the owner of the technology desires Stevens to commercialize the technology.
In such cases, the technology should be submitted using the Technology Disclosure Form.
Copies of disclosures which are made to other parties must be submitted simultaneously to ORS as well.

This will allow coordination of actions between Stevens and the other party with regard to the seeking of intellectual property rights in accordance with the obligations expressed in the research agreement or contract.
Typically, this situation may occur when a Stevens researcher is part of a team whose funding is administered by another institution or by a government laboratory.

Responsibilities of the Patent Committee: The Patent Committee shall have the following powers and duties: to meet from time to time as necessary to discharge its duties, with due regard for the fact that valuable patent rights in the United States and foreign countries can be lost if patent applications are not filed in a timely manner; to evaluate each invention-disclosure report submitted to it, with such expert assistance as may be necessary, and to report its findings and recommendations with respect to each such report to the President; to determine with respect to each invention-disclosure report submitted to it the relative equities or rights held by the inventor(s), the Institute, and any sponsoring or cooperating agencies, and, if necessary, to negotiate agreements among all parties concerned with respect to such equities or rights; to determine with respect to each inventor for each technology-disclosure report whether the inventor has executed an agreement to assign invention and patent rights to the Institute and to clarify the rights of the inventor(s) under the terms of that agreement; to recommend with respect to each invention-disclosure report whether or not the Institute should bear the costs in obtaining, enforcing, maintaining, and marketing patent rights in the invention which is the subject of the invention-disclosure; to authorize applications for patents and to retain patent counsel for matters pertaining to the filing of patent applications, the prosecution thereof, and any litigation that may arise therefrom, subject to approval by the President; to instruct OTT as to its determinations with regard to disclosures and patent maintenance issues so that OTT can assist in the implementation of its decisions; to release patent rights in an invention to the inventor or inventors when deemed appropriate, subject to the inventor(s) granting a shop-right to the Institute; to oversee the collection of royalties and fees pertaining to inventions, patents, and patent applications and the distribution thereof to those entitled thereto; to cooperate with appropriate Institute officers in negotiations to obtain from cooperating or sponsoring agencies agreements concerning patent rights to inventions or discoveries made as a result of research carried on under grants or contracts from the cooperating or sponsoring agencies; in its consideration of matters relating to each particular patent situation, the Patent Committee shall seek the advice of patent counsel where appropriate; to coordinate all consulting agreements, research agreements, or other agreements to which the Institute is a party which may involve the possibility of patents or discoveries by the faculty, staff, or other employees; after a total of $20,000 has been expended for the direct costs of obtaining, enforcing, maintaining, and marketing patent rights in an invention for which the Institute has accepted the responsibility for all or a portion of such direct costs, the Patent Committee shall review the status of the case and make a presentation to the President before any further expenditures are made; to make such reports to the Board of Trustees or its designees as the Board may direct.

Operational Guidelines: The Patent Committee reviews Technology Disclosures submitted by Stevens faculty, staff, and students to determine patentability and potential research and commercialization opportunities of technology.
If an invention is made which may be subject to the Institute's Patent Policy, the inventor(s) should complete a Technology Disclosure for submission to the Patent Committee.

The Technology Disclosure is reviewed for completeness and to identify any imminent deadlines which could affect patent rights, such as publication, presentations, or meetings with a potential commercial sponsor.
While timely disclosures by faculty are strongly encouraged, in the case of an imminent deadline, expedited review and decision making is possible.

If an invention is made in the course of a project funded by a federal agency, Stevens is required to notify the funding agency within two months of the submission of a Technology Disclosure to Stevens.
Accordingly, an invention which involves federal funding may be handled on an expedited basis.
In the normal course, a technology is usually initially reviewed and receives a preliminary evaluation by the Patent Committee within three months of the submission of a Technology Disclosure.
Generally, the preliminary evaluation by the Patent Committee will include inviting inventor(s) to a Patent Committee meeting.

After the preliminary evaluation by the Patent Committee, a patentability evaluation may be assigned to a patent attorney for advice to the Patent Committee concerning the potential patentability and scope for an invention.
The results of the patentability evaluation are presented at a Patent Committee meeting and a decision about the filing of a patent application may be made.

If the Patent Committee decides that more information is needed to make a determination about filing an application, from either a patent law or technical or commercial feasibility standpoint, the decision may be deferred.
In most cases, the Patent Committee endeavors to make a decision within a year of receiving a Technology Disclosure.

However, a decision may be deferred for up to two years after the date that the Technology Disclosure was submitted, unless there is a statutory period, such as publication, presentation, or foreign filing deadline, or federal patent rights involved.

For inventions made with federal funding, Stevens is required to provide at least sixty days notice to the funding agency prior to the end of a statutory period if it does not wish to pursue patenting and commercializing an invention.
For an invention made with federal funding, a decision about patenting and commercializing a technology must be made no later than two years after disclosure to the federal agency.

If the Patent Committee decides that it does not wish to pursue an invention, rights may be offered back to the inventor pursuant to the Patent Policy, and subject to any federal patent rights or contractual obligations to other funding organizations.
Patent Protection: Stevens will normally seek patent protection on inventions in order to pursue commercial licensing and to comply with the terms of sponsored research agreements.
Stevens often will not seek protection for inventions which are not commercially attractive, even if the invention is intellectually meritorious, unless otherwise requested by the sponsor.

Publication or Presentation: It is important, however, to understand that any presentation, public disclosure, use, sale, offer-to-sell, or thesis defense which describes an invention even in minimal detail prior to filing for a patent may preclude patenting in foreign countries and may also preclude protection in the United States unless a patent is filed within one year from publication.

The implications of publication upon patent rights should be discussed with ORS or with OTT and a decision on patent filing reached promptly so that delays in presentation and/or publication can be avoided.

Waiver of Stevens' Rights: It is Institute policy that if the Patent Committee decides not to pursue intellectual property protection on a technology, Stevens will grant to the inventor(s) rights to the technology subject to a right for Stevens to use the technology for its own use (shop-right).
Stevens may consider releasing an invention to the inventor(s), if so requested.
Any such decision must be approved by the President upon the recommendation of the Vice President for Research Services and the Patent Committee.
In the case of industrial sponsorship, Stevens will seek approval of the sponsor prior to releasing its ownership rights in favor of the inventor.
Decisions regarding applications for patents, copyrights, etc. for donated technologies will be the responsibility of the Patent Committee.
Copyright protection of books, articles, and publications is sought in order to recognize authorship and protect the integrity of the work.
It is also essential in order for Stevens to license copyrightable materials to commercial book publishers and others and to comply with the terms of sponsored research agreements.
A copyright is established at the time expression is fixed in a tangible medium, whether or not it is officially registered.

If a work is Stevens-owned, as defined in Section 2 of this Guide, then the following notice must be prominently affixed to the copyrighted material: "Copyright (c) Year STEVENS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY.
The date in the notice should be the Year in which the work is first published.
No notice other than the foregoing is to be used for Stevens-owned works.
In the case of software, a copy of the notice should be included in the source code near the top of the listing as well as on the user's screen when execution begins.
If being distributed on transportable digital media, a printed label should be affixed with the notice (e.g., on magnetic media such as diskettes).
Further, for added copyright protection, certain works should be registered with the United States Copyright Office using its official forms.
The Patent Committee will decide when registration is appropriate.
Questions concerning copyright notices and registration should be brought to OTT.

Federal research agreements presently vary widely with respect to rights in copyrightable technical data and computer software, but in general, universities have the right to copyright and to control distribution of most materials.
Several major agencies retain a large degree of control over computer software and will relinquish control only under limited circumstances, usually to be negotiated as part of the contract or grant.
This is one of the reasons why it is required that all such agreements be reviewed in advance by ORS.

When it has the right to do so, Stevens may, if requested by the author(s) and at Stevens' discretion, "stand aside" in those situations where Stevens believes that it would enhance the transfer of technology to the public, is consistent with Stevens' obligations to third parties, and does not involve a conflict of interest as set forth below.
By "standing aside," Stevens agrees not to exercise its contractual rights to the technology, clearing the way for the Stevens author(s) to maintain ownership.
In the case of industrial sponsorship where the sponsor acquires license rights, Stevens will seek approval of the sponsor prior to releasing its ownership rights in favor of the author.
A trade or service mark may be used to protect those names and symbols associated with certain Stevens activities and events and with certain technology developments such as computer programs.
Prior to registration for trademark protection, the designation "TM" after a trademark or "SM" after a service mark will give adequate notice of a claim of ownership.
The designation "(r)" for a trademark may only be used after Federal registration.

The use of trade and service marks to protect Stevens-owned technology or to designate Stevens as the origin of a product, event, activity, service, or the like, may be instituted only with the approval of the Vice President for Research Services.
It is important to note that trademark protection carries with it certain obligations on the part of the holder of the mark.
Therefore, requests for use and registration of trade or service marks on behalf of Stevens must be referred to ORS.
Protection of a mask work commences with the registration of its initial commercial exploitation.
If registration for protection has not been made within two years of the initial commercial exploitation, mask work protection may be lost and the work entered into the public domain.

To protect mask work rights, the following notice is to be applied on all Stevens-owned semiconductor chip products which incorporate mask works: "Mask work M, or (M), STEVENS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY."
It is the responsibility of the researcher who produces or who has such masks produced to assure that this notice is affixed to the mask work.
Questions concerning mask work notices and registration should be brought to OTT.
Tangible research property (TRP) such as biological materials and computer software are frequently patented or copyrighted as appropriate and then licensed for commercial purposes.

However, these and other forms of TRP, including those under commercial license, generally are simultaneously distributed solely for research purposes either under simple letters of understanding, Materials Transfer Agreements, or more formal licenses.
The following sections deal only with dissemination of TRP for research and other non-commercial purposes.
Commercial licensing of TRP is covered in Section 4.
In keeping with the traditions of academic science and its basic objectives, it is the policy of Stevens that results of scientific research are to be promptly and openly made available to others.

Since the traditional modes of dissemination through scholarly exchange and publication are not fully effective for most TRP, it is Stevens' policy that those research results which have tangible form should also be promptly and openly made available to other scientists for their scientific research, unless such distribution is inappropriate due to factors such as safety, the need to more fully characterize or develop the TRP prior to distribution, or unless such distribution is incompatible with other obligations.

The letter of transmittal or Materials Transfer Agreement which accompanies distributed TRP must contain a disclaimer of warranties, a statement that the materials are to be used for research purposes only, and that they are solely for the use of the recipient who may not further distribute the TRP without the express written permission of Stevens Institute of Technology.
OTT has prepared a standard Materials Transfer Agreement which may be used for this purpose.

Where TRP is developed in the course of research which is subject to the terms of a sponsored research or other agreement, control over its development, storage, distribution, and use is the responsibility of the principal investigator.
In other cases, significant use of Institute resources will be presumed, so control over TRP rests jointly with the Academic Dean and the Vice President for Research Services.
The responsibility for control includes determining if and when distribution of the TRP is to be made beyond the laboratory for scientific use by others in accordance with the terms of this policy.

TRP may have potential commercial value as well as scientific value, and the principal investigator who may wish to make TRP available for scientific use in a manner which does not diminish its value or inhibit its commercial development should seek guidance from OTT.
The normal mechanism for commercialization of TRP is through licensing agreements as set forth in Section 4 of this Guide.
Each item of TRP should have an unambiguous identification code and name sufficient to distinguish it from other similar items developed at Stevens or elsewhere.
OTT can provide assistance in developing appropriate identification systems.
Biological materials are in many cases patentable and licensed for commercial purposes under various types of patent licenses.
They are also a form of tangible research property which can be distributed for commercial and/or research purposes with or without patent protection.
Biological TRP owned by Stevens may usually be distributed for research purposes only, with minimal conditions attached.
Any such distribution is subject to an agreement by the recipient that commercial development or commercial use or further transfer of the biomaterial is not to be undertaken.
An example of such an agreement for use of biomaterials may be found in the Appendix to this policy ("Materials Transfer Agreement").
In addition, the principal investigator may wish to control subsequent use, for example, by requiring recipients to follow a specific research protocol in the use of the biological materials.

When distributing biological TRP to research colleagues outside the laboratory, costs of the materials and handling may be recovered from the recipient, and returned to the account which funded those costs.
When costs are charged for TRP distribution, adequate documentation must be maintained for audit purposes.

If there is a possibility of biohazard or other risk associated with the transport, storage, or use of a particular biological TRP, or if the recipient is likely to use the TRP for clinical research, OTT should be contacted for advice on the appropriate form of disclaimers of liability and indemnities.

If the biological TRP was developed under a sponsored research agreement, OTT should be contacted to advise on possible contractual obligations with respect to the TRP prior to its distribution for non-commercial purposes.
Distribution of biological TRP which is part of a patent or patent application should be coordinated through OTT.

The distribution of Stevens-owned computer software to colleagues for research purposes must have the approval of the Vice President for Research Services if the software has potential commercial value, if the principal investigator wishes to control subsequent use, or if it is subject to the terms of a sponsored research agreement.

For the distribution of non-commercial software, the following notice should be included: "Copyright (c) Year STEVENS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY.

Once a Technology Disclosure Form disclosing an invention, copyright, etc. is submitted, OTT typically will meet with the inventor(s) as a first step in evaluation.
In many cases, contact with industry will be made as a part of the evaluation process.
Evaluations will be submitted to the Patent Committee for its use during deliberations on the disclosure.
The determination as to how to pursue protection for an invention or other intellectual property rests upon multiple criteria.
Broadly speaking, these fall under the categories as to whether the invention can be patented and whether it can be licensed.
The former is decided by obtaining a professional opinion from a patent attorney.
The licensing criteria include the answers to questions such as: What is the invention's primary application?
Are there other uses to which the invention can be put?
How does the invention compare with the current solutions?
How many related patents are there, or is there significant patent activity in the field?
Even if it is patented, would it be enforceable, e.g., can infringers be identified; is it distinguishable from alternative approaches?
Are the sponsors of the research interested in licensing the invention?
Is the industry predisposed for or against licensing?
Who will derive the value from the invention (i.e., customers, third-party resellers, licensees, sublicensees, etc.)?
Has the inventor had previous success with technology transfer and/or industry?
Is there a "champion" for the invention, and if so, who?
Is it an extension of a related commercial success?
Do customers and distribution channels already exist?
What are the commercialization opportunities and what is the likelihood of commercial success?
What is Stevens' relationship with that industry and discipline?
Is there financial support from licensees or sponsors?
What potential complications are there to licensing the invention?
How much monitoring and maintenance will a license require?
Experience proves that the inventor's insights and assistance are extremely valuable in the evaluation process.
Stevens considers the inventor's availability for consultations with OTT to be important.

10.8.1 Patent Policy Policy Number and Name: 10.8.1 Patent Policy Approval Authority: Board of Trustees Responsible Executive: Provost Responsible Office: Office of the Provost Effective Date: December 16, 2014 I.
Preamble Stevens is dedicated to teaching, research, and the expansion of knowledge.

While Stevens encourages research and related activities for their intrinsic value, it recognizes that inventions and discoveries, and related know-how, may result from various activities conducted wholly or in part at Stevens or under Stevens auspices.

It is Stevens policy to promote the use of inventions for the public good and, where appropriate, to pursue patents and commercialization opportunities to encourage development and marketing of such inventions.

This Patent Policy expresses Stevens commitment to promoting research and scholarship as well as to facilitating the development, dissemination, and commercialization of inventions and discoveries, and related know-how, for the greatest public benefit.
Under applicable Federal law, an invention is, as a general matter, a new and useful discovery, process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.

If a patent is granted with respect to an invention, the patent owner will have the right to exclude others from the manufacture, use or sale of the invention, and may license those rights to others for a limited period of time provided by law.

This patent policy defines ownership rights relating to inventions and discoveries and ensures that the proceeds from any commercialization are distributed to members of Stevens community who make inventions covered by this Policy, and to their schools, their departments and Stevens, in a manner consistent with the research and other objectives of Stevens.

This Policy also aims to assist members of the Stevens community in complying with Stevens obligations under the Bayh-Dole Act (relating to federally funded research), as well as in complying with obligations resulting from Stevens acceptance of research funding from other sponsors.

Stevens may have obligations to seek patent protection and to commercialize inventions made in the course of federally sponsored research in accordance with the terms of federal patent policy regarding such inventions.

For all inventions and discoveries which are subject to the Patent Policy, it is within Stevenss sole discretion to determine whether to seek patent protection and to pursue commercialization of such inventions and discoveries.

Stevens has created the Office of Innovation and Entrepreneurship within the Office of the Provost, which is responsible for managing all activities relating to the protection and commercial promotion of intellectual property.

Scope and Applicability; Duty to Disclose This policy applies to the following categories of persons: Faculty (full-time and part-time, including faculty who elect to be paid on a nine-month basis), visiting faculty who conduct research, whether paid or unpaid, research scientists and post-doctoral appointees, students (including visiting students), other employees (full-time and part-time), including professional staff, technical employees and clerical employees, and non-employees who participate in research at Stevens or research carried out under the auspices of Stevens, such as scholars who do not have a faculty appointment, fellows, and consultants.

Each person covered by this Policy has a continuing obligation to promptly disclose to Stevens every invention and discovery covered by this Policy including without limitation any know-how related to such inventions and discoveries, and inventions and discoveries arising in the course of consulting activities, and to execute and deliver to Stevens such assignments and other forms of documentation as may be necessary or appropriate to further effectuate the terms of this Policy.
All disclosures under this Policy shall be made to the Office of Innovation and Entrepreneurship, as set further described in Section VIII.B.

Ownership of Inventions and Discoveries Full-time Employees, including faculty, research scientists, post-doctoral appointees, and staff: Stevens will own any inventions conceived or first reduced to practice by full-time employees in the course of University employment or with substantial use of University resources.

Stevens will not claim ownership of an invention that was conceived and first reduced to practice as part of a consulting agreement or employment arrangement with an outside organization, if certain conditions are met, or during an unpaid leave.
Generally speaking, for faculty members and other academic appointees, the phrase course of University employment refers to their Field of Appointment, as defined in Section III.G below.

Part-time Employees, including faculty, research scientists, post-doctoral appointees, and staff: Inventions conceived or first reduced to practice by part-time employees are the property of Stevens if an invention was conceived or first reduced to practice in the course of University employment or with substantial use of University resources.

University Faculty on Leave and/or Visiting Other Institutions: In general, inventions conceived or first reduced to practice by University faculty during a paid leave (whether at Stevens or elsewhere, including another institution or a company) are the property of Stevens, but inventions conceived and first reduced to practice by University faculty during an unpaid leave are not the property of Stevens, unless substantial use of University resources was involved.

If conception of an invention occurred during an unpaid leave and reduction to practice occurred by the faculty member after the faculty members return to Stevens, the invention is wholly or partially the property of Stevens, depending on the circumstances under which the invention was conceived and reduced to practice.

Similarly, if conception of an invention occurred before the leave began and reduction to practice occurred while the faculty member was on leave, the invention is wholly or partially the property of Stevens, depending on the circumstances under which the invention was conceived and reduced to practice.

In cases in which there are potential conflicts between Stevens policies and those of an institution at which faculty will be on leave and/or visiting, such conflicts shall be resolved through good faith negotiations between Stevens and such institution before the leave begins.
Non-Employees and Visitors: It is not unusual for visitors from other institutions to participate in research or other research-related activities at Stevens or under Stevens auspices.
Such participation by a visitor might result in inventions or discoveries.

Each such visitor shall be subject to this Policy and inventions and discoveries made by such a visitor shall be owned by Stevens, unless agreed otherwise in writing by Stevens and the home institution.
Undergraduate and Graduate Students: This section applies to students enrolled at Stevens and non-enrolled students who are visiting Stevens.
In general, students shall retain ownership of inventions conceived or first reduced to practice as part of class work.

When a student conceives or first reduces to practice or contributes to the conception of an invention in the course of internally or externally sponsored research, including research for the students thesis or dissertation, any research involving substantial use of University resources, participation as a team member in a University-based research project involving other students, faculty or staff, research that is substantially directed by a faculty member or researcher employed by Stevens including without limitation a thesis or dissertation, or employment at Stevens, Stevens shall own such invention and the student shall share in the proceeds, if any, as an inventor in accordance with Section V.

It is recognized that students working individually or as part of a team of students on a Senior Design Project which involves a problem or question initiated and framed by a third party sponsor may make substantial use of University resources.

Given the significance of Senior Design to the educational process of students at Stevens and the legitimate interests of sponsors, inventions conceived or first reduced to practice by one or more students in the course of a Senior Design Project shall be owned by the individual or group of students and, upon written agreement of all students in a Senior Design Project and following disclosure of the invention to Stevens, such students may license or transfer rights owned by such students in and to the invention to the sponsor, whether prior to or following graduation.
Alternatively, upon written agreement of all of the students in a Senior Design Project and Stevens, the students may assign their rights in such invention to Stevens under this Policy.
Any inventorship rights of a faculty member shall be determined by the general rules applicable to faculty inventions.
If the Senior Design student group assigns rights to a sponsor, the expectation in most circumstances will be that Stevens will license the interest of the faculty member to the sponsor.
Consultants Hired by Stevens: Inventions conceived or first reduced to practice in the course of a consultants paid consulting work for Stevens shall be the property of Stevens.
Consultants should be hired only pursuant to a prior written agreement in a form approved by Stevens.
This provision will, as a general matter, apply to consultants who conduct research or create content for Stevens and not apply to the purchase of goods and services by Stevens.
Definitions: Field of Appointment refers to the broad academic field or area of research activities in which a faculty member is engaged.

Primary indicators include, but are not limited to, the academic unit or department in which the faculty member is appointed or closely related departments, or any area in which the faculty member might conduct research as part of his/her academic appointment. Substantial Use of University Resources The precise determination of what usage of Stevens resources or assistance of non-faculty personnel shall be considered substantial, or when the identity of a project resides with Stevens rather than with particular individuals, involves the exercise of judgment based on the circumstances and on practices within the discipline.

As a basic principle, however, use of Stevens resources or assistance from non-faculty personnel that is incidental and not essential to the development of the invention does not constitute substantial use.

Thus, for example, none of the following shall be considered substantial use: use of resources or personnel commonly available to faculty in the same school, institute or department, such as libraries, offices, desktop computers, or secretarial staff; occasional use of a specialized piece of equipment or facility for routine tasks; receipt of salary by faculty for their academic appointments; and the use of resources or facilities generally available to all students as part of their educational activities.

Examples of use of Stevens resources which will be considered substantial include use of a specialized laboratory by a PhD student, use of student employees or researchers by a faculty member, and research conducted by a team under departmental or school auspices.

Outside Consulting Activities of Faculty All full-time faculty have the ability to engage in some amount of outside consulting activities in accordance with the policies contained in the Stevens Faculty Handbook.

Prior to beginning outside consulting activities, faculty shall inform the party for whom the consulting activities are to be performed of this Patent Policy and the faculty members obligations under this Policy.

In order to enable faculty to engage in permissible consulting while at the same time delineating Stevens interests in conducting corporate sponsored research, Stevens will make no claim to an invention made by a faculty member in the course of a disclosed consulting engagement if the invention resulted from work on a specific problem or topic proposed by the company or entity to which the faculty member is consulting and on which problem or topic the faculty member is not engaged in active research at Stevens, and the invention was conceived and first reduced to practice without the use of Stevens resources or personnel.

Note that this is a more restrictive standard than Substantial Use. A faculty member may agree to assign inventions made in the course of consulting to the company or entity only if these conditions are satisfied.
If these conditions are not able to be satisfied, faculty are encouraged to consult the Office of Sponsored Programs to determine whether corporate sponsorship is an appropriate alternative.
Faculty are required to disclose inventions made in the course of consulting to Stevens to determine if such conditions are met.

Commercialization of Patents When Stevens owns the patent rights to an invention and the inventor has signed the Stevens Patent Agreement, the inventor has the right to share in the proceeds derived from commercializing the patent and any related know-how.

Stevens will make an initial allocation from gross proceeds, if any, in the aggregate amount of $25,000 to fund a research account at Stevens to support academic research activities of the inventor or inventors of a particular invention hereunder.

Following the allocation contemplated by the previous paragraph, all distributions shall be based upon net proceeds and shall ordinarily be distributed as follows: fifteen percent for the general support of the Office of Innovation and Entrepreneurship and to cover any other expenses associated with the commercialization of Stevens inventions, and the remaining net proceeds shall be distributed as follows: fifty percent of net proceeds to the inventor or inventors for the first $5,000,000 of net proceeds, forty percent of net proceeds in excess of $5,000,000 and not exceeding $10,000,000, and thirty percent of all amounts of net proceeds in excess of $10,000,000.

The remainder of net proceeds shall be used by Stevens for research, scholarship and other educational activities in the following manner: forty percent to the school or other Stevens division in which the invention was made, twenty percent to the Office of the Provost, and forty percent to Stevens.

Gross proceeds are all proceeds from licensing or otherwise granting rights in an invention to third parties, including license fees, royalties on sales or other usage, and milestone payments, but excluding research funding and any reimbursement for patent prosecution expenses.
Net proceeds are gross proceeds minus all out-of-pocket expenses incurred by Stevens that are directly associated with the particular invention.

Out-of-pocket expenses may include patent expenses, legal expenses associated with negotiating an agreement, travel expenses, payments due to other parties with rights in the invention, or any other reasonable out-of-pocket expenses incurred in pursuing Stevens patent rights.

If Stevens pursues or defends litigation to enforce patent rights, then the proceeds of any judgment or settlement from such litigation shall ordinarily be included in gross proceeds, and the associated litigation expenses shall be deducted as out-of-pocket expenses.
If litigation is pursued, the distribution described above may be modified to reflect the greater economic risk being incurred by Stevens in pursuing such litigation.

In the event of any litigation, actual or imminent, or any other activity to enforce or defend patent rights, Stevens may withhold distribution of and retain royalties or other payments received until such matters are resolved.
The funds so withheld shall be placed in income producing investments during such period, determined in the discretion of the Office of Finance.

After any such matter is finally resolved, Stevens shall undertake a final accounting and, within thirty days thereafter, the share of the inventor or inventors in the funds so withheld and in the accrued income shall be distributed to the inventor or inventors, subject to prior recovery of costs and overhead as specified above.

Inventors who are employees of Stevens, acting within the course of such employment and not faculty or research staff, will not automatically be covered by this Section; rather, in such cases, the Administrative Council of Stevens, following a recommendation from the supervisor of such an employee or the relevant project leader, shall make a determination as to the appropriateness of such employee sharing in the proceeds of commercialization.

Equity received from a company or other entity in lieu of license fees or royalties shall be allocated by calculating and distributing the appropriate number of shares, using the percentages outlined above, irrespective of their value, provided that any inventor who holds an equity position in the company or other entity shall not share in Stevens equity and any inventor(s) who does not hold an equity position in the company or entity shall, for purposes of distribution, receive fifty percent of such equity.
In the event there is a single share or a partial share which cannot be distributed to the inventor(s), that share or partial share shall belong to Stevens.

Unless otherwise required by contractual arrangements or applicable law, Stevens shall distribute shares of equity at the time they are received by Stevens or will require that the inventor receive such equity directly from the company or other entity.

In the event that Stevens is required to hold the shares for any length of time or is otherwise restricted from distributing shares to inventors, Stevens shall hold such shares or other interests but shall not be responsible for any fluctuation in the value of the shares or any matters relating to the administration of such shares or interests.
Shares of proceeds shall be used by departments, schools and Stevens to further the research, scholarship and educational goals of Stevens.

If more than one inventor is to share in the inventor share, the inventors shall decide among themselves their respective shares and shall provide the Office of Innovation and Entrepreneurship with a written agreement signed by all inventors.

Preamble Stevens is dedicated to teaching, research, and the expansion of knowledge.

While Stevens encourages research and related activities for their intrinsic value, it recognizes that inventions and discoveries, and related know-how, may result from various activities conducted wholly or in part at Stevens or under Stevens auspices.

It is Stevens policy to promote the use of inventions for the public good and, where appropriate, to pursue patents and commercialization opportunities to encourage development and marketing of such inventions.

This Patent Policy expresses Stevens commitment to promoting research and scholarship as well as to facilitating the development, dissemination, and commercialization of inventions and discoveries, and related know-how, for the greatest public benefit.
Under applicable Federal law, an invention is, as a general matter, a new and useful discovery, process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.

If a patent is granted with respect to an invention, the patent owner will have the right to exclude others from the manufacture, use or sale of the invention, and may license those rights to others for a limited period of time provided by law.

This Patent Policy defines ownership rights relating to inventions and discoveries and ensures that the proceeds from any commercialization are distributed to members of Stevens community who make inventions covered by this Policy, and to their schools, their departments and Stevens, in a manner consistent with the research and other objectives of Stevens.

This Policy also aims to assist members of the Stevens community in complying with Stevens obligations under the Bayh-Dole Act, as well as in complying with obligations resulting from Stevens acceptance of research funding from other sponsors.

Stevens may have obligations to seek patent protection and to commercialize inventions made in the course of federally sponsored research in accordance with the terms of federal patent policy regarding such inventions.

For all inventions and discoveries which are subject to the Patent Policy, it is within Stevenss sole discretion to determine whether to seek patent protection and to pursue commercialization of such inventions and discoveries.

Stevens has created the Office of Research, Innovation and Entrepreneurship within the Office of the Provost, which is responsible for managing all activities relating to the protection and commercial promotion of intellectual property.

Scope and Applicability; Duty to Disclose This Policy applies to the following categories of persons: Faculty (full-time and part-time, including faculty who elect to be paid on a nine-month basis), visiting faculty who conduct research, whether paid or unpaid, research scientists and post-doctoral appointees, students (including visiting students), other employees (full-time and part-time), including professional staff, technical employees and clerical employees, and non-employees who participate in research at Stevens or research carried out under the auspices of Stevens, such as scholars who do not have a faculty appointment, fellows, and consultants.

Each person covered by this Policy has a continuing obligation to promptly disclose to Stevens every invention and discovery covered by this Policy including without limitation any know-how related to such inventions and discoveries, and inventions and discoveries arising in the course of consulting activities, and to execute and deliver to Stevens such assignments and other forms of documentation as may be necessary or appropriate to further effectuate the terms of this Policy.
All disclosures under this Policy shall be made to the Office of Research, Innovation and Entrepreneurship, as further described in Section VIII.B.

Ownership of Inventions and Discoveries Full-time Employees, including faculty, research scientists, post-doctoral appointees, and staff: Stevens will own any inventions conceived or first reduced to practice by full-time employees in the course of University employment or with substantial use of University resources.

Stevens will not claim ownership of an invention that was conceived and first reduced to practice as part of a consulting agreement or employment arrangement with an outside organization, if certain conditions are met, or during an unpaid leave.
Generally speaking, for faculty members and other academic appointees, the phrase course of University employment refers to their Field of Appointment, as defined in Section III.G below.

Part-time Employees, including faculty, research scientists, post-doctoral appointees, and staff: Inventions conceived or first reduced to practice by part-time employees are the property of Stevens if an invention was conceived or first reduced to practice in the course of University employment or with substantial use of University resources.

University Faculty on Leave and/or Visiting Other Institutions: In general, inventions conceived or first reduced to practice by University faculty during a paid leave, whether at Stevens or elsewhere, including another institution or a company, are the property of Stevens, but inventions conceived and first reduced to practice by University faculty during an unpaid leave are not the property of Stevens, unless substantial use of University resources was involved.

If conception of an invention occurred during an unpaid leave and reduction to practice occurred by the faculty member after the faculty members return to Stevens, the invention is wholly or partially the property of Stevens, depending on the circumstances under which the invention was conceived and reduced to practice.

Similarly, if conception of an invention occurred before the leave began and reduction to practice occurred while the faculty member was on leave, the invention is wholly or partially the property of Stevens, depending on the circumstances under which the invention was conceived and reduced to practice.

In cases in which there are potential conflicts between Stevens policies and those of an institution at which faculty will be on leave and/or visiting, such conflicts shall be resolved through good faith negotiations between Stevens and such institution before the leave begins.

Such participation by a visitor might result in inventions or discoveries.

Each such visitor shall be subject to this Policy and inventions and discoveries made by such a visitor shall be owned by Stevens, unless agreed otherwise in writing by Stevens and the home institution.
